title: Prayer as rhythm
hookLine: Muslim daily prayer gives the whole day five fixed moments to come back to

lines: STILL DARK. A CALL, A CHIME.
AGAIN AT NOON. AGAIN AT SUNSET.
cards: It's still dark. A call to prayer drifts from a minaret, or a phone chimes softly on a nightstand. Someone gets up, washes face, hands and arms, wipes the head, washes the feet, turns toward Mecca, and stands.
A few minutes later, the day begins. Just after noon, in an office or a stockroom, it happens again. In the afternoon, again.
Just after sunset. And once more at night. Between are meetings and school runs, dishes and traffic.
The prayer doesn't replace any of that. It stitches it together.

teach.b: Day two hundred sixty-eight brought the five daily prayers; today, their rhythm. The Arabic word is salah. In one place the Qur'an ties it to the clock: prayer, it says, is prescribed for believers at set times.
The number comes from the hadith.
In a long account in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is given fifty prayers a day on the Night Journey.
On the advice of Moses he goes back, again and again, to ask for fewer, until they stand at five.
Muslims name them by their hour: fajr at dawn, dhuhr after midday, asr in the afternoon, maghrib after sunset, isha at night.
The times follow the sun, so they drift through the year, set not by a boss or a calendar but by the sky. Another hadith gives the rhythm a picture.
The Prophet asks his companions: if a river ran past your door, and you bathed in it five times a day, would any dirt be left on you? None, they say.
That, he tells them, is what the five prayers are like: through them God washes away wrongs.
Inside each prayer is a rhythm too: standing, reciting, bowing, going down with the forehead to the ground, sitting, and up again.

teach.h: PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS.
teach.b: In every prayer the opening chapter of the Qur'an is recited, which begins, in Pickthall's English: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." A rule tells you what to do. A rhythm tells you when to come back.

how: Muslims pray salah five times a day at times set by the sun, from dawn to night, after washing and facing toward Mecca; each prayer moves through standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, and the opening chapter of the Qur'an is recited in every one.

o: prayer said whenever you feel moved to pray
salah, kept at five set times that move with the sun
one long prayer said once a week at the mosque

practice: This isn't salah, and it isn't meant to stand in for it; it's a way to notice the shape of your own day.

Walk through it in your mind, waking, the middle of the day, the afternoon, the light going at sunset, the last minutes before sleep, and at each one ask where you already pause and where you rush straight through.
If you pray, notice where a prayer already lives, or could.

wordCard.voice: Prayer as rhythm. Salah, the Muslim daily prayer, kept at five moments that move with the sun, giving the whole day places to return to. Today's word.
